plan.question: How did a hidden invasion force collapse in just three days?

chapters.title: The Hidden War
beats: In April 1961, 1,400 armed men landed on a remote Cuban shore, backed by the world's most powerful intelligence agency. Their goal was to spark a popular uprising that would topple Fidel Castro’s government.
The invasion was orchestrated by the United States, a response to Castro’s alignment with the Soviet Union and his reforms that threatened American business interests in Cuba.
But the uprising never came. Within three days, the invaders were defeated, their defeat broadcast live around the world.
The Bay of Pigs was meant to be a bold covert success. Instead, it became a national humiliation for the United States and a turning point in global Cold War tensions.
This is the story of how a secret war went wrong—and why it still echoes decades later.

chapters.title: The Players
beats: Fidel Castro rose to power in 1959 after leading a revolution that overthrew dictator Fulgencio Batista. He became Prime Minister and began transforming Cuba with land reforms and nationalizations.
Castro believed in revolution first, elections later—a stance that alarmed the United States, which had long influenced Cuban politics.
Dwight D. Eisenhower, then U.S. president, saw Castro as a communist threat and authorized covert plans to remove him, funding anti-Castro exiles and training them for sabotage.
His successor, John F. Kennedy, inherited the invasion plan but hesitated to fully commit air support, fearing public backlash if the operation was exposed.
At the heart of the operation was Richard Bissell, a CIA official who had spent years building a paramilitary brigade from Cuban exiles, believing they could trigger mass resistance.
On the Cuban side, General José Ramón Fernández commanded the Revolutionary Army’s counteroffensive. Loyal to Castro, he mobilized rapidly to crush the landing.
Cuba itself, just south of Florida, had become a symbolic battleground between Cold War rivals, its fate tied to the superpowers watching from afar.

chapters.title: The Plot Thickens
beats: By early 1960, President Eisenhower began contemplating ways to remove Castro, seeing his shift toward the Soviet Union as a direct threat to U.S. interests.
In February of that year, CIA officers devised a plan to sabotage Cuban and American sugar mills, aiming to destabilize the economy.
By March, the CIA presented its full plan for Castro’s overthrow to the National Security Council, proposing an armed invasion supported by air strikes.
Castro responded by aligning more closely with the Soviet Union, ordering Cuban oil refineries to process Soviet crude oil.
In return, the U.S. canceled its import of Cuban sugar, deepening the economic rift between the two nations.
As tensions mounted, Castro condemned elections as corrupt, while dissent brewed within his own ranks when army commander Huber Matos accused him of 'burying the revolution.'
Meanwhile, former minister Manuel Artime reached out to the American embassy, helping the CIA recruit and train Cuban exiles for the invasion.

chapters.title: The Invasion Begins
beats: On April 15, eight CIA-supplied B-26 bombers struck Cuban airfields, hoping to destroy Castro’s air force on the ground.
But the planes attacked too late in the day and missed key targets, leaving much of the Cuban air force intact.
Two days later, on April 17, the main invasion force landed at Playa Girón in the Bay of Pigs, expecting to meet little resistance.
Instead, they were met by a well-prepared Cuban force under General José Ramón Fernández, who had anticipated the assault and positioned troops accordingly.
Without air cover and facing coordinated ground resistance, the invaders quickly realized their assumptions about a popular uprising were wrong.

chapters.title: The Collapse
beats: Over the next three days, the Cuban Revolutionary Army pressed forward, cutting off retreat routes and capturing key positions around the Bay of Pigs.
General Fernández coordinated his forces with precision, using intelligence gathered from earlier raids and defectors to outmaneuver the invaders.
Fidel Castro arrived at the front lines, rallying his troops and declaring that counter-revolutionaries would be defeated on Cuban soil.
The invading force, isolated and overwhelmed, sent desperate pleas for U.S. air support that never came.
On April 20, the remnants of the brigade surrendered, their banners lowered and their mission in ruins.

chapters.title: The Cost of Failure
beats: President Kennedy took full responsibility for the disaster, calling it a grave error that damaged American credibility worldwide.
The failed invasion strengthened Castro’s grip on Cuba and pushed him closer to the Soviet Union, setting the stage for the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962.
That same year, the U.S. imposed a trade embargo on Cuba, sealing the island’s economic isolation for decades.
In later years, the Church Committee revealed that the CIA had also plotted multiple times to assassinate Castro, exposing the depth of U.S. opposition.
For Castro, the victory at the Bay of Pigs confirmed his belief in revolutionary resistance—and ensured his defiance would endure long after the dust settled.
